PullRequest.Title: editTelemetry: release consumed document snapshots
PullRequest.Body:
Fixes #345244.

The edit-change stream used a replaying `AsyncIterableSource`, retaining full-document snapshots after consumption. Repeated edits to a large document therefore caused unbounded memory growth.

- Use the existing non-replaying `AsyncIterableProducer` without changing the shared async API.
- Subscribe synchronously and buffer only changes that arrive before the producer starts; clear that startup buffer after transferring it.
- Preserve edit ordering, transaction metadata, queue draining, and disposal behavior.
- Add regression tests for those behaviors and garbage collection while the document-processing pipeline remains active.

RegressionFixes.Mechanism: A replaying AsyncIterableSource retained every emitted change object, including both full StringText document snapshots, after the sole consumer had processed it; retained memory therefore grew with edit history for as long as document telemetry tracking remained active.
RegressionFixes.Symptom: Repeated edits, especially in large long-lived documents, caused monotonically growing retained heap and corresponding GC pressure.
RegressionFixes.FixedBehavior: The changed helper now returns a single-consumer AsyncIterableProducer. Its ProducerConsumer removes each consumed value from _unconsumedValues, while the startup buffer is explicitly cleared after transfer, so only pending changes remain retained and consumed full-document snapshots can be collected.
RegressionFixes.Evidence: Base line 33 constructed AsyncIterableSource for iterateObservableChanges; AsyncIterableSource delegates to AsyncIterableObject, whose _results array appends every emitted change and whose iterator advances only a private index, so consumed entries remain referenced for the stream lifetime. CombineStreamedChanges creates this stream per tracked document and each change includes value/prevValue StringText snapshots. The added GC regression test drives 80 edits while the pipeline remains active and requires all 40 sampled consumed snapshots to be collectible.

Scenarios.Scenario: Ordinary typing and inline edits in a tracked open document
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The observable change callback synchronously enqueues a value/prevValue snapshot, then returns; the single async consumer publishes non-chat, non-external edits without awaiting an expensive boundary, so telemetry processing is off the editor input critical path after enqueue.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Edit frequency and the number/size of pending document snapshots for one tracked document; effective retained cardinality is queue backlog rather than total edit history.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: One AsyncIterableProducer consumer and one serialized _run loop per document; edits arriving while the consumer is busy remain ordered in the producer queue. Different documents are independent.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: There is no cache or cache key. Before the producer microtask starts, synchronous changes use a short startup buffer that is transferred and cleared; afterward changes go directly to the producer. Consumed entries are removed rather than replay-cached.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed helper is directly invoked by CombineStreamedChanges, and AsyncIterableProducer removes consumed queue entries while preserving only pending edits.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The exact memory benefit depends on document size, edit frequency, and document lifetime; the changed mechanism itself is clear and does not add work proportional to consumed history.
Scenarios.Verdict: No regression. The diff removes history-sized retention; ordinary edits add only bounded enqueue/dequeue work and no new boundary call.

Scenarios.Scenario: Streamed chat edits and disk-reload edits that require diff computation
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Changes are enqueued, then CombineStreamedChanges serially groups chat changes or handles each external reload and awaits editor-worker diff computation before publishing. The worker call was already on this path; the diff only replaces the in-process stream queue.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Compute a string edit diff in the editor worker via IEditorWorkerService.computeStringEditFromDiffWithMetadata.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One call per completed streamed-chat group and one call per external reload change; ordinary user edits make zero calls.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same CombineStreamedChanges loop made the same worker calls with the same grouping and serialization; only consumed queue retention changed.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The serialized consumer awaits this result before publishing the corresponding annotated edit; later edits can queue behind it.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Effective cardinality is chat groups plus individual reloads, with pending edit count during an active worker diff controlling temporary memory.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Per document, _run awaits one diff at a time. Chat edits are coalesced over the existing one-second window; external reloads remain one diff per observable reload change. Backlog accumulates only while the current serialized operation is pending.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No diff-result cache is present. Chat edits use existing temporal coalescing; reloads intentionally remain separate. The new producer retains pending snapshots during a slow worker call but releases them after consumption.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for unchanged worker-boundary behavior and reduced consumed-snapshot retention; medium for maximum real-world backlog magnitude.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Backlog size depends on edit bursts and worker latency, but the diff neither increases worker-call cardinality nor concurrency. AsyncIterableProducer uses array shifts for backlog draining, yet realistic backlog is bounded by the serialized diff window and does not establish a high-confidence regression.
Scenarios.Verdict: No introduced performance issue. Existing worker IPC remains serialized and unchanged, while consumed full-document snapshots are now released.

Scenarios.Scenario: Document shutdown and waitForQueue drain/restart boundaries
Scenarios.CriticalPath: waitForQueue clears the old run store, completes its stream after already queued edits, waits for the existing serialized run to drain, runs the boundary callback, and starts the next stream. Disposal may wait for an already-started worker diff but adds no new boundary.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of edits already queued at the boundary; retained state falls as the single consumer drains it.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: _runQueue serializes the previous consumer, the drain callback, and the replacement consumer. Store disposal synchronously unsubscribes and resolves the producer; no parallel drain burst is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache. Queued pre-disposal changes are drained in order; post-boundary changes enter the newly created producer. Startup buffers are cleared after transfer and completion wakes a pending reader.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: lifecycle ordering is explicit in _restart, DeferredPromise completion, and the added queue/disposal tests.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Drain duration depends on pre-existing queued edits or an in-flight worker diff, but the changed completion mechanism does not add a new wait or repeated operation.
Scenarios.Verdict: No regression. The new lifecycle releases consumed values and preserves serialized draining without new I/O, IPC, or concurrency.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all three changed files and traced the only production caller through editing, diff-worker, queue-drain, and disposal paths. No diff-introduced performance finding met the reporting threshold. The PR is itself a high-confidence fix for unbounded full-document snapshot retention, recorded against introducing commit 22440e0276be6fa9554868660a41dff33785d5e6.
